title: Who Were the Vikings?
description: What the word meant, the shock of Lindisfarne, and the raiders who came before it

concepts.title: A Job, Not a People
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with the word. Old Norse had two related nouns: a víkingr was a person, while víking was an activity.1 Runic inscriptions and skaldic praise poems from the period suggest that a víkingr was someone who went on expeditions, usually abroad, usually by sea and usually in a group. The word implied no particular ethnicity and could describe your own crew as easily as someone else's. As the historian Judith Jesch points out, the activity could certainly include raiding, but was not restricted to it.

So going viking was something people did, not something they were. Most people in the Viking Age north fished, farmed, traded and made things. The scholar Brian McMahon puts it this way: going viking was something a man might do in his youth to win honour and plunder, and it was rare for anyone to raid abroad throughout his life. The darker sense of predatory pirates is clearest in the Icelandic sagas, written two or three centuries later, and it is the sense modern English inherited.

Here is a surprise: the English word is modern. "Viking" entered Modern English in 1807, in an age of growing nationalism and empire,2 and Sir Walter Scott was an early adopter. People who actually met the raiders used other labels, most of them not ethnic at all: wicing, rus, pagani (pagans), pirati (pirates).

Historians now use Viking more broadly, for people of Scandinavian origin or connections who traded and settled as well as raided, inside and outside Scandinavia, between about 750 and 1100. As you will see, that world also absorbed many people who were not Scandinavian at all. You met the Vikings briefly in Exploration and Maritime; this topic goes deeper into the evidence and the arguments.

concepts.title: Lindisfarne, 793
concepts.contentHtml:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle sets the scene for 793 with omens over Northumbria: "immense sheets of light rushing through the air, and whirlwinds, and fiery, dragons flying across the firmament." A great famine followed. Then "the harrowing inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc in the church of God in Holy-island, by rapine and slaughter." Holy Island is Lindisfarne, just off the Northumbrian coast, where St Cuthbert had been bishop and where his body was revered as a saint's. English Heritage dates the attack to 8 June,1 although the Chronicle in the translation quoted here gives a January date: even famous dates need checking.

It was not the first raid on England. A few years earlier, in 789, three ships of northmen landed on the coast of Wessex and killed the king's reeve, the official sent to bring the strangers to court; the Chronicle says he did not know what they were. What made Lindisfarne a shock was the target: the sacred heart of a Christian kingdom.

News reached Alcuin, a Northumbrian scholar working as tutor to Charlemagne's children. He wrote to Higbald, bishop of Lindisfarne, that the church of St Cuthbert was "spattered with the blood of the priests of God". For Alcuin the disaster "has not happened by chance, but is the sign of some great guilt." He may have had a scandal in mind. Sicga, who had led the murder of King Ælfwald in 788 and later killed himself, had been buried on Lindisfarne just six weeks before the raiders came.

In letters to English kings, Alcuin also scolded the English for copying their attackers: "Look at your trimming of the beard and hair, in which you have wished to resemble the pagans." The raiders, it seems, were already setting fashions.

concepts.title: Before Lindisfarne: The Salme Ships
concepts.contentHtml:
Lindisfarne is the traditional start of the Viking Age, which historians often bracket as 793 to 1066. But on the Estonian island of Saaremaa archaeologists found something older. In 2008 and 2010 they uncovered two ship burials near the village of Salme. The first held seven men aged between 18 and 45. The second, a boat 17.5 metres long, held 34 men stacked four high.

The Salme II bones showed multiple stab and cut wounds from sharp-edged weapons. Archaeologists read the graves as Swedish warriors, buried rapidly in their boats after a battle, sometime around 750: decades before Lindisfarne. The grave goods fit an elite war party far from home: swords and shields, knives, whetstones and combs, whalebone playing pieces for the board game hnefatafl, and even dogs and hunting hawks.

Science then filled in the people. Isotopes in their teeth pointed to the Mälar Valley in Sweden. Ancient DNA, analysed for the 2020 Viking genomes study, showed that four of the men in Salme II were full brothers, and that the rest of the dead came from the same district.1 An early raiding party, it seems, was a local affair: neighbours and family in one boat.

Salme also redraws the map. Some of the earliest raiders in the archaeological record were heading east across the Baltic, not west to England. In the eighth century the Baltic was already a place where Scandinavians, Frisians, Slavs and Arab merchants were in frequent contact, so the raids grew out of a busy world of exchange rather than appearing from nowhere. Why raiding took off when it did is still debated.

title: Ships and Navigation
description: How the Oseberg and Gokstad ships were built and sailed, and the sunstone debate

concepts.title: Oseberg and Gokstad
concepts.contentHtml:
Much of what we know about early Viking ships comes from a handful of rich burials around the Oslo Fjord in Norway. Two stand out.

The Oseberg ship was built of oak in south-western Norway in the 820s. It is 21.5 metres long and 5 metres wide, with 15 oar holes on each side, enough for a crew of 32: thirty rowers, a helmsman and a lookout. After about 14 years at sea it was hauled ashore for the last time and became the burial ship of two women in 834.1 Nobody knows who they were, but the sleighs, wagon, carved animal heads, textiles, beds and tents buried with them show that one or both held an important political or religious role. Here is the twist. In the later tenth century grave robbers broke in, hacked the carved serpent head off the prow and threw it deeper into the grave. That vandalism saved it: left in place, it would probably have rotted away.

The Gokstad ship, found in the King's Mound at Gokstad farm in 1880, was built around 890 and used for a powerful man's burial around 900. It is 23 metres long, clinker-built with 16 strakes of overlapping planks, with 16 oar holes a side and room for a crew of perhaps 67. With its sail raised and a good wind it could probably reach 11 knots, about 20 kilometres an hour. Its deep hull was built for the open, rough sea, and its museum suggests such ships could have carried settlers, tools and even animals west.

Be careful about what these ships represent. They are elite burials, and the Oseberg ship, the earliest preserved Scandinavian sailing ship, was not yet as capable at sea as later vessels. Wood rarely survives, so our picture of ordinary ships is patchy.

concepts.title: Built From the Shell Inwards
concepts.contentHtml:
Viking shipwrights worked in a tradition centuries old. The Nydam boats from Denmark, from about 350 CE, already show the clinker (or lapstrake) technique, in which each hull plank overlaps the one below. The builder laid the keel and stems first, then added overlapping planks one by one, riveting each to its neighbour. Only then were ribs inserted inside to stiffen the hull. This shell-first method remained the normal way to build ships in northern Europe until the late Middle Ages.

The planks were not sawn. With no saws in northern Europe until the thirteenth century, craftsmen split tree trunks instead,1 shaping each plank for its place in the hull. Oak was the first choice; in the north, where oak did not grow, pine was used. Iron for rivets and tools was easy enough to obtain that a reasonably wealthy farmer could build himself a ship.

The sail is the surprise. Scandinavians had used oared boats for centuries, but sails only reappeared there towards the end of the seventh century, probably through growing trade with northern Europe. Oars, sail and a shallow draught together made a ship that could cross open sea, run up rivers and drop raiders close to targets as far inland as Paris.

By the tenth century ships were specialising. Cargo ships like those from Hedeby, dated to about 1025, might have carried as much as 60 tons with a small crew. Warships grew long and slim. The Viking Ship Museum in Roskilde counts a ship as a longship only if it is at least five times as long as it is wide, and the longest known, Roskilde 6, built after 1025, is 36 metres long.

concepts.title: Finding the Way, and the Sunstone Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
Vikings crossed the North Atlantic without a magnetic compass, charts or logs. On long passages they island-hopped, or tried to stay within sight of known landmarks, and they read the sun and stars, the waves and winds, the way clouds behave over land, and the movements of birds and sea mammals. It did not always work: Erik the Red, who colonised Greenland, lost more than half his ships on his first journey there.

Northern summer skies are too light for stars, and fog or cloud could hide the sun for days. In the late 1960s the Danish archaeologist Thorkild Ramskou proposed an answer. One saga tells how King Olaf, on a snowy, overcast day, asked a man named Sigurd where the sun was; Sigurd held a sunstone up to the sky and saw where the light came from. Ramskou suggested the sunstone was a crystal such as calcite, cordierite or tourmaline, used to read the pattern of polarised light in the sky and so locate the hidden sun.

It is an elegant idea, and a popular one, but it is a hypothesis. A team at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, led by Gábor Horváth, noted that it had been widely accepted and cited despite a total lack of experimental evidence,1 and the saga never says what the stone actually was. So they tested it, first with volunteers in a laboratory and a planetarium, then in a 2018 simulation of 1,000 three-week voyages from Norway to Greenland. Dénes Száz and Horváth found sky-polarimetric navigation surprisingly successful even in cloudy weather, provided the navigator found north at least once every three hours.2

Notice what that shows. The method could have worked; it does not prove that Vikings used it. A fragment of a wooden disc from southern Greenland, scratched with curved lines, has been read as part of a sun compass, but how navigators used it is reconstructed rather than recorded.

title: From Raiding to Ruling
description: The Great Army, Normandy's founding deal and Cnut's North Sea empire

concepts.title: The Great Army and the Repton Dead
concepts.contentHtml:
After decades of hit-and-run raids, the scale changed. In 865 a Great Army, led by Halfdan and Ivar the Boneless, landed in East Anglia. York fell in 867. By 871 the army had beaten every force sent against it, and Alfred of Wessex paid it to leave his kingdom. These were no longer summer raiders but an army that stayed through the winter, took land and set up kings.

In 873 the army wintered at Repton in Derbyshire and drove the Mercian king into exile. Excavations at St Wystan's Church in the 1970s and 1980s found Viking graves and, under a low mound, a charnel deposit of nearly 300 people. One room held the mixed bones of at least 264 individuals:1 about 80 per cent men, mostly aged 18 to 45, several with violent injuries, and around 20 per cent women. With them lay an axe, knives and five silver pennies dating from 872 to 875.

Then came a puzzle. Radiocarbon dates suggested the bones had collected over several centuries, so they could not all belong to the army. In 2018 Cat Jarman and colleagues explained why: the dead had eaten plenty of fish. Carbon from the sea is older than carbon in land foods, and this marine reservoir effect makes bones look too old. Once it was corrected, every date fitted the late ninth century.2 Jarman stayed careful: the dates do not prove these were members of the army, but it now seems very likely.

The army's campaigns ended in a partition. After Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878, England was divided between Wessex and the region known as the Danelaw. The Place Names topic shows how thickly Norse names settled there. The lesson here is that bones, coins and isotopes can test the chronicles directly.

concepts.title: Normandy: The Deal of 911
concepts.contentHtml:
Francia suffered the same pattern. Viking raids there began in 820, with ships making easy incursions up the Seine; in 841 raiders sacked and burned Rouen, and in 845 Charles the Bald paid a Viking army to end a siege of Paris. Frankish rulers had paid off Danish raiders for almost a century. Then, in about 911, King Charles the Simple struck a different kind of bargain with a chieftain called Rollo: land of his own, in return for defending it. Rollo was baptised, taking the name Robert, and married the king's daughter Gisla, under what is called the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte. His land became Normandy, the land of the Northmen, with its capital at Rouen.

How do we know? Mostly through Dudo of Saint-Quentin, whose history of the Normans was commissioned by Rollo's grandson Richard I. Dudo is the first writer to record anything about Rollo, and he had access to Rollo's immediate descendants and to documents since lost. But he also polished a raider into a model Christian ruler. His most famous scene: asked to kiss the king's foot, Rollo refused and ordered one of his warriors to do it. The man lifted the foot to his mouth while standing upright and tipped the king flat on his back, to roars of Viking laughter. Treat it as a story with a point, not as minutes of a meeting.

Even Rollo's origins are disputed. Dudo made him a Dane; a Norwegian origin appears in the eleventh century, was popularised in the twelfth and was taken up by the Icelandic writer Snorri Sturluson. There is still no consensus.

One popular belief is simply wrong. Rollo is often called the first Duke of Normandy, but he never held that title: the first duke was his great-grandson Richard II.1 His great-great-great-grandson was William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy and, from 1066, King of England.

concepts.title: Danegeld and Cnut's North Sea Empire
concepts.contentHtml:
In the late tenth century large Viking fleets returned to England, and the English tried paying. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that in 991 it was resolved that tribute should be given to the Danes for the first time, "for the great terror they occasioned by the sea-coast", and that the first payment was 10,000 pounds. By 1012 the price was 48,000 pounds. Then the payers acquired a Danish king. In 1016 Cnut, son of the Danish king Swein Forkbeard, defeated Edmund Ironside at Assandun; Edmund died a few weeks later, and Cnut became king of England. In 1018 the whole country paid 72,000 pounds, plus 10,500 from the citizens of London,1 after which part of the army sailed home to Denmark and forty ships stayed with Cnut.

Cnut then built a North Sea empire. He succeeded his brother as king of Denmark in 1018 and took control of Norway in 1028 after ousting Olaf Haraldsson. He married Emma of Normandy, widow of the English king Æthelred, and in 1027 travelled to Rome for the imperial coronation of Conrad II, securing lower tolls for English pilgrims. For a time England was not just next to the Scandinavian world but part of it.

Now the famous story. Cnut supposedly sat on the beach and ordered the tide to stop, and his name became shorthand for deluded arrogance. The tale was recorded by Henry of Huntingdon in the 1100s, and in that version the point is the opposite: Cnut shows his flattering advisers that he is not all-powerful, because only God is.2 The legend began as praise of a wise and pious king.

The empire did not outlast him. Cnut died in 1035, Norway returned to its old dynasty and his line in England and Denmark ended in 1042. In 1066 the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada pressed his own claim to England and died at Stamford Bridge, the year historians often use to close the Viking Age.

title: The Eastern Routes
description: The Rus, Ibn Fadlan's eyewitness account, Arab silver and the Varangian Guard

concepts.title: Who Were the Rus?
concepts.contentHtml:
The Kievan Rus lesson in Russian and Soviet History told the chronicle story: Scandinavian princes, Rurik at Novgorod, a new seat at Kyiv. Here you look at the evidence behind the name Rus, and it is slipperier than it looks.

Start with the genes and the towns. The 2020 Viking genomes study found a Swedish influx into the Baltic, while Danish ancestry flowed into England and Norwegian into Ireland, Iceland and Greenland. The Salme brothers of Lesson 1 are an early example of that eastward movement. Trading towns such as Birka, on the Swedish island of Björkö, belonged to a network that reached beyond the Ural Mountains into the Caliphate and south to the Byzantine Empire.

But the people outsiders called Rus may not have been a single ethnic group. In his annotated translation of the most famous Arabic account, the Cambridge Arabist James Montgomery sets out four possibilities. The Rus could be Scandinavians, specifically an elite of eastern Swedish merchant-pirates operating out of Ladoga and Rurik's hill-fort.1 They could be a local people named after the river Ros. The account could blend Slavic and Scandinavian groups that Arab writers did not tell apart. Or they could be a people in the middle of changing, as Scandinavian newcomers adapted and assimilated. Scholars he quotes argue that Arab authors gave the word no ethnic meaning, using it for warriors and merchants whatever their origin.

The same caution applies in the west, where contemporaries' labels such as wicing, rus and pagani described what people did rather than who their ancestors were. Keep that in mind as you meet the Rus through the eyes of one remarkable visitor.

concepts.title: Ibn Fadlan on the Volga
concepts.contentHtml:
In 921 the caliph al-Muqtadir in Baghdad sent an embassy to the king of the Volga Bulghars, who had asked him for help. Its secretary, Ahmad ibn Fadlan, wrote an account of the journey. On the river Atil, the Volga, he met a people he calls the Rus, who had arrived on a trading expedition.

He begins with admiration: he had never seen more perfect physiques; they were like palm trees, fair and reddish, and every man carried an axe, a sword and a dagger. Their women wore neck bands of gold and silver that worked like a bank statement: a man had one made for his wife when his wealth reached ten thousand dirhams, another at twenty thousand, and so on. The Rus brought slave girls to sell, and paid a dirham apiece for dark-green ceramic beads.

Then comes disgust. He calls them the filthiest of God's creatures, because they did not wash after relieving themselves or when ritually impure. Every morning a slave girl carried a single basin of water round the house;1 each man washed his face and hair in it, combed his hair, blew his nose and spat into it, then passed it on. Notice the yardstick: Ibn Fadlan judged by Islamic rules of ritual purity.

His longest passage describes a chieftain's ship funeral. For a rich man, a third of his wealth went on drink for the funeral. One of his slave girls agreed to die with him, and once she had said so she could not turn back; after days of ritual she was killed and burned beside him on his ship. A Rus bystander told the interpreter, "You Arabs are a foolish lot!": Arabs buried their dearest to be eaten by worms, whereas fire sent them straight to paradise.

How far can you trust it? Scholars Montgomery quotes note that this was one rich man's cremation, held in Russia under foreign influences, that some details came only through an interpreter, and that features such as an old woman called the Angel of Death have no parallel in Norse sources.

concepts.title: Silver Roads and the Emperor's Guard
concepts.contentHtml:
What drew Scandinavians east was, above all, silver. In 1999, at Spillings in Othem on the Swedish island of Gotland, the largest surviving Viking Age silver hoard in the world came to light. It weighed 67 kilograms and had been hidden under the floor of a large building, probably in cloth sacks. It held about 14,300 coins and masses of silver arm rings and armlets; the youngest coins were struck in the 870s, and most came from the Islamic Caliphate.1 These Arab silver coins, dirhams, were the currency Ibn Fadlan counted in. Gotland alone accounts for about two-thirds of all the Viking Age silver coins found in Sweden, some 168,000, mostly Arabic, English and German.

Others went east to serve. Around 988 the Byzantine emperor Basil II, facing rebellion, received 6,000 Rus warriors from Vladimir of Kyiv, and was so impressed that he made them his personal bodyguard: the Varangian Guard. Harald Hardrada spent a decade in it before becoming king of Norway. The pay was legendary: one modern historian describes their right, on an emperor's death, to take as much gold from the treasury as they could carry. And a twist: after 1066 many Anglo-Saxons joined, and by the thirteenth century most of the guard was English.2

They left their names behind. On a gallery of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, then the world's largest building, a Norseman scratched runes reading "...alfdan drew these runes". On both sides of a great lion outside the Arsenal in Venice, which once stood in the Athens port of Piraeus, someone carved Scandinavian runes. At home, a runestone at Ed north of Stockholm says of Ragnvald, "He was in Greece, he was the chief of the warrior party", Greece meaning the Byzantine Empire. Uppsala University's database of runic inscriptions includes finds from Russia, Ukraine and Turkey.

title: The North Atlantic
description: Dating the settlement of Iceland and Vinland, and why Norse Greenland came to an end

concepts.title: Dating the Settlement of Iceland
concepts.contentHtml:
Iceland's own historians supplied a date. Ari fróði's Íslendingabók, the Book of the Icelanders, says that Ingólfur Arnarson probably first reached land at Reykjavík around 870. Settlers came from Scandinavia and the British Isles, pushed, the traditional account says, by land shortage and internal disputes in Norway. Exploration and Maritime gave you that date. The question here is how you test a date written down long afterwards.

Volcanoes help. Icelandic eruptions spread layers of ash, called tephra, across the country, and each layer is a time marker: a turf wall built on top of it is younger, anything sealed beneath it is older. The key marker is the Landnám tephra layer, from landnám, "land-taking". Greenland ice cores dated it to 871 ± 2 in one core and 877 ± 4 in another, and recent work uses 877 ± 1. Two later ash layers, from 939 and about 938, give further fixed points.

In a 2017 study Magdalena Schmid, Andrew Dugmore, Orri Vésteinsson and Anthony Newton reassessed 300 Viking-period settlement sites, 253 of which could be dated with tephra. The Landnám layer and the two later ashes appear at 58 per cent of those 253 sites. Their conclusion is precise: colonisation had started before the 870s in the south-west, but the bulk of first settlement came after that date.1 Environmental records from the south-west suggest people and livestock arriving some time between 830 and 877.

What about claims of settlers around 700? A dozen or so radiocarbon dates pointed that way, but their positions in the ground are insecure or their interpretation is demonstrably wrong. One supposedly early date even comes from a layer above the 877 ash, which suggests the settlers were burning old dead timber, wood that had died long before it reached the fire. Here science confirms the written tradition in outline while sharpening it.

concepts.title: Vinland, Exactly 1021
concepts.contentHtml:
Exploration and Maritime told you that Norse voyagers reached North America around 1000 and that L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is their only confirmed site. Here is how we know, and how precisely.

The written story comes from two Icelandic sagas set down in the thirteenth century, The Saga of the Greenlanders and Erik the Red's Saga, together called the Vinland sagas. They disagree: in the first, Bjarni Herjólfsson is blown off course and sights a forested land that Leif Erikson later explores; in the second, Leif himself is blown off course. In the early 1960s the Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad found what he thought were Norse buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows, and his wife Anne Stine Ingstad led excavations there from 1961 to 1968. Finds included a soapstone spindle whorl, a sign that women were present, and butternuts, which grow not there but further south around the Gulf of St Lawrence: evidence of voyages beyond the camp.

The date was the problem. More than 150 radiocarbon dates had been obtained, 55 of them from the Norse occupation, yet their ranges spread across the entire Viking Age. In 2021 Margot Kuitems, Michael Dee and colleagues used a sharper clock. In 993 a sudden burst of cosmic radiation raised the carbon-14 in the atmosphere, and the spike appears in tree rings all around the world. They found it in three pieces of wood from the site, from three different trees and at least two species, all cut with metal tools that the local Indigenous people did not make. Counting rings from the spike to the bark edge gave the same felling year every time: 1021. One tree was cut in spring, another in summer or autumn.

That makes 1021 the only secure calendar date for Europeans across the Atlantic before Columbus1 and, as the authors note, the first known point at which humans had encircled the globe.

concepts.title: Why Norse Greenland Ended
concepts.contentHtml:
Norse Greenland began in 985 and lasted until the middle of the fifteenth century. Its people lived mainly by raising livestock on cleared pasture, and the population may have reached about 2,000. It was farming at the limit: cattle spent the winter in dark byres, and by spring many were too weak to walk, so farmers carried them out to pasture. The Western Settlement was abandoned in the fourteenth century, the Eastern Settlement in the fifteenth. The last written evidence is a record of a wedding at Hvalsey Church in the early fifteenth century; radiocarbon dates suggest about half a century more of occupation.

Why did it end? The popular answer is the cold of the Little Ice Age. The evidence is more interesting. In 2022 Boyang Zhao, Raymond Bradley and colleagues reconstructed climate from the sediments of a lake beside a Norse farm and found no substantial temperature change during the settlement period.1 Instead the region grew steadily drier, which would have cut the grass needed to feed livestock through the winter, and the drying coincides with a shift in the Norse diet.

In 2023 Marisa Borreggine and colleagues added a counterintuitive twist. As the southern Greenland ice sheet readvanced, its growing gravitational pull on the ocean and the sinking of the crust beneath it raised local sea level by up to about 3.3 metres, flooding coastal land and forcing people off many coastal sites.2

Trade mattered too. Ancient DNA from walrus ivory found in Europe, analysed by Bastiaan Star, James Barrett and colleagues in 2018, shows the trade shifting from mainly eastern sources to almost exclusively Greenland ivory. European use of walrus ivory peaked in the twelfth century and then declined. A colony that leaned on one luxury export was resilient while demand lasted and vulnerable when it fell. Research now points to a combination of environmental and economic pressures rather than one killer cause.

title: Law, Women and the Written Word
description: Thing assemblies, women's power, the Birka warrior debate, runestones and the sagas

concepts.title: The Thing: Assemblies and Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Norse communities settled disputes and made law at open-air assemblies called things. The best documented is Iceland's Althing. You met it in Gods That Died, at the dramatic conversion of about 1000; here is how it worked.

After settlement, Icelanders first set up district assemblies at Þórsnes and Kjalarnes. Shortly before 930 the chieftains sent a man named Úlfljótur to Norway to learn laws and customs that could serve as a model, and in 930 people gathered at Þingvellir for the first Althing. The site came with a grim legal footnote: according to Íslendingabók, a landowner there, Þórir Kroppinskeggur, murdered his servant, and as punishment all his land passed into common ownership for the assembly's use.

The central figure was the Law Speaker. He memorised the laws and recited all of them in instalments over three years, going over the procedural rules every summer. The Law Speaker was chosen by the Lögrétta, the legislative assembly, for a three-year term and was the only paid official of the Commonwealth:1 the most powerful person in the country while the assembly met, and officially powerless the rest of the year. At the Law Rock, Lögberg, anyone attending could step forward and present a case. The Commonwealth lasted from 930 until Icelanders swore allegiance to the Norwegian king in 1262.

Things met across the Norse world. On the Isle of Man the parliament, Tynwald, traces its origins to the things of the Viking Age, and Tynwald Hill at St John's is one of four known Viking assembly sites on the island. The hill is an artificial mound, with sods of earth from each parish forming its tiers. Tynwald celebrated its millennium as a continuous parliament in 1979, and every 5 July the year's new laws are still proclaimed from the hill in English and Manx.

concepts.title: Women's Power and the Birka Warrior
concepts.contentHtml:
Many people picture the Viking Age as a man's world. The archaeologist Marianne Moen argues that this picture owes a lot to the nineteenth century, when Victorian ideals of women belonging to the home were imposed on Viking society. Women were often buried with keys, a sign of their responsibility for, and perhaps control over, the running of the household; as Moen puts it, the large estates were seats of power and the woman of the house had the keys. Some runestones were commissioned by women, alone or jointly. And some 40 graves in Scandinavia and beyond lend credence to saga stories of female sorceresses, the völur, who could see into the future and were associated with a staff.

Then there is grave Bj 581 at Birka, excavated in 1878 by Hjalmar Stolpe. It held a sword, an axe, a spear, armour-piercing arrows, a battle knife, two shields, two horses and a full set of gaming pieces: the kit of a high-ranking professional warrior. The skeleton was taken to be male until an osteological study suggested otherwise; in 2017 Charlotte Hedenstierna-Jonson and colleagues sequenced the genome. There was no Y chromosome: the warrior was a woman.1

Critics claimed the team had studied the wrong bones, or that the grave was a double burial made for a missing man. In a 2019 reply in Antiquity, Neil Price and colleagues pointed out that Stolpe's 1879 report says the grave contained a single body, and every bone of the skeleton is individually labelled "Bj.581" in ink.2 A third thigh bone in the storage box is labelled "Bj.854": it had strayed from another grave. The authors suggested that behind many objections lay the assumption that a female warrior was a contradiction in terms.

Some questions stay open. No injuries from fighting were found on the skeleton, and the 2017 paper itself asks whether weapons necessarily make a warrior. One overview of Viking women judges that excitement over the find seemed to overtake caution. The genome settles her biological sex; the social role she lived, her gender, is a separate and harder question.

concepts.title: Runestones and Sagas: Weighing the Witnesses
concepts.contentHtml:
Two kinds of Norse writing survive, and they have opposite strengths.

Runestones are contemporary. Sweden has about 2,600 Viking Age runestones, mainly in the provinces around Lake Mälaren,1 against about 60 in Norway and about 220 in the Danish lands. Most follow a memorial formula, X raised this stone in memory of Z, their relative, and they were normally commissioned by wealthy families. Some are signed by their carvers, of whom Åsmund, Fot and Öpir are the best attested. One of Öpir's, now in the University Park in Uppsala, reads: "Gullaug had the bridge made for the spirit of Gillaug, her daughter". Uppsala University's Runor database lists over 7,000 runic inscriptions worldwide, and Viking Age stones were often raised for people who had died overseas. The drawback is that the texts are laconic: who raised the stone, for whom, sometimes where the dead fell.

Sagas are the opposite: long, vivid and late. The Icelandic sagas were written two or three centuries after the events they describe, and they shaped the predatory modern meaning of "Viking". Can they be trusted? The Vinland sagas are a test case. They disagree about who found America, yet L'Anse aux Meadows shows that they remembered real voyages, at least partly, through oral tradition. They also had agendas. Erik the Red's Saga may magnify Thorfinn Karlsefni and his wife Gudrid at Leif's expense, perhaps because a thirteenth-century movement sought sainthood for their descendant, Bishop Björn Gilsson.2

So historians read a saga the way a detective reads a statement taken long after the event: good evidence for what a community remembered and valued, risky for exact details, and always checked against archaeology, runestones and outside witnesses such as Ibn Fadlan or the English chroniclers.

title: Myth Versus Evidence
description: Horned helmets, skull cups, Viking hygiene and what ancient genomes reveal

concepts.title: Where the Horns Came From
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask anyone to draw a Viking and you will probably get horns. The evidence says no. The best-preserved Viking helmet in the world was found in 1943 at Gjermundbu in Ringerike, Norway, in the cremation grave of a very wealthy man. Made between 950 and 975, it is a spiked iron helmet with "spectacles" guarding the eyes and nose, and complete it would have weighed about 1.5 kilograms. It has no horns. Only two other helmets are known from Viking Age Scandinavia, and such helmets were expensive; few warriors could afford one. The Museum of the Viking Age in Norway is blunt: Viking battle helmets never had anything as impractical as horns.1

Horned figures do appear in art from before and during the Viking Age, on helmet decorations, fittings and tapestries such as the one from Oseberg, but they are weapon dancers, gods or monsters, not ordinary fighters.

So where did the horns come from? One clear source is Carl Emil Doepler, costume designer for the premiere of Wagner's Ring of the Nibelung at the Bayreuth Festival in 1876.2 The Swedish painter Johan August Malmström also put horned helmets into his illustrations of the Norse sagas. Such artists may have been inspired by real ancient horned helmets being discovered at the time, which later proved to be far older than the Vikings.

The most famous real horned helmets were found later still. In 1942 a peat cutter at Viksø in Denmark dug up pieces of two bronze helmets; thinking they were rubbish, he set them aside. In 2019 a researcher spotted birch tar inside one horn, and radiocarbon dating put the helmets at 1006 to 857 BCE. They were deposited in the bog around 900 BCE, in the Nordic Bronze Age, roughly 2,000 years before the Viking Age, and they were never used for battle.

concepts.title: Combs, Baths and Skull Cups
concepts.contentHtml:
Second myth: Vikings were filthy. Archaeology disagrees. Viking graves and settlements are full of combs, tweezers and razors, found beside both men and women. Combs, carved from antler, bone, ivory and wood and often kept in their own cases, were so common that almost every Viking seems to have carried one. The poem Hávamál agrees, advising you always to go out with your hair combed, even if you cannot afford good clothes.

The best testimony comes from enemies. The thirteenth-century English chronicler John of Wallingford, justifying the massacre of Danes in England in 1002, complained that the Danes made themselves too attractive to English women:1 "They combed their hair every day, bathed every Saturday, and even changed their garments often." Back in the 790s, Alcuin had already scolded the English for copying pagan hairstyles.

Yet in Lesson 4 Ibn Fadlan called the Rus the filthiest of God's creatures. Both can be true. He judged by Islamic rules of ritual purity and was revolted by a shared washbasin; the English judged by their own standards and found the Danes vain. Who counts as dirty depends on who is doing the judging.

Third myth: Vikings drank from their enemies' skulls. This one has a precise origin. In 1636 Ole Worm, court physician to the Danish king and a keen student of runes, published a Norse poem in which a warrior expects to drink ale in Valhalla from the "curved branches of skulls", meaning the horns growing from animals' heads. Worm translated the phrase into Latin2 as ex craniis eorum quos ceciderunt, "from the skulls of those they killed", and a mistranslation became a reputation. The blood eagle, a supposed ritual of opening a living victim's back, is shaky too. It first appears in skaldic verse; Roberta Frank argues it grows more lurid with each passing century; and a recent anatomical study concluded that a living victim would have died early in the procedure.

concepts.title: What the Genomes Say
concepts.contentHtml:
Finally, the most dangerous myth: that Vikings were a single, pure, blond Nordic people. Nineteenth-century writers praised Vikings as ancestor figures for European colonists, Nazi ideology nurtured the idea of a Germanic master race, and white supremacists still borrow the image. Ancient DNA lets you test it directly.

In 2020 a team of about 90 researchers led by Ashot Margaryan and Eske Willerslev published the genomes of 442 people from archaeological sites across Europe and Greenland, most of them from the Viking Age. Among the findings:

  • Gene flow into Scandinavia from southern Europe and Asia, before and during the Viking Age.
  • Genetic differences between regions within Scandinavia, with restricted gene flow between them.
  • Different diasporas: Danish ancestry into England, Swedish into the Baltic, Norwegian into Ireland, Iceland and Greenland.
  • Many Vikings had brown rather than blond hair.
  • Two men buried with swords in Viking-style graves on Orkney were genetically similar to present-day Irish and Scottish people, and could be the earliest Pictish genomes yet studied.1

That last result matters most: people with two genetically British parents received Viking burials in Orkney and Norway. As the Uppsala archaeologist Charlotte Hedenstierna-Jonson put it, being a Viking was a cultural rather than genetic affiliation.2 That fits what the word meant in Lesson 1.

Two cautions. Genes track ancestry, not occupation, so they cannot tell you who actually went viking. And results can pull in different directions: the 2015 People of the British Isles study, discussed in the Place Names topic, found no clear Danish genetic signature in the old Danelaw, while the 2020 study reports a major influx of Danish ancestry into England. Different samples, different methods and the genetic closeness of Danes and Anglo-Saxons all shape the answer, which is why the Ancient DNA topic spends so long on method.
